content:
Hi everyone, I have been trying to understand how to properly work with partial derivatives and differentials inside PhysLib, in a way that is as close as possible to the way we do derivatives in physics.

I've looked at Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/FDeriv, which might be the best one. However, it's clearly done the math way. Do people know something better, in that it is closer to the physics way of doing things? What about working with differentials?

Would it make sense to have a syntactic wrapper around FDeriv that it brings the notation and handling closer to the physics way?

I've been working on something but I'm relatively new so my rate of progress is definitely limited

For derivatives, we have the wrappers Space.deriv Time.deriv and SpaceTime.deriv, and some lemmas around these. These are not defined as general as they could be (e.g. they are defined with fderiv not with mfderiv).

For differentials, we currently don't have anything. I'm not sure of the status of this in Mathlib?

I wrote this guide on partial derivatives in mathlib as it comes up from time to time. You might find it useful https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/113489-new-members/topic/partial.20derivative.20of.20a.20vector.20field/near/506481684

Thank you @Joseph Tooby-Smith and @Tomas Skrivan ! I really liked the guide on partial derivatives you wrote @Tomas Skrivan and I agree with some of the comments you made in that conversation, that we should be making an effort to bridge between the hard formality of lean and the ease of notation people are used to. Especially physicists. I'm going to try and take a crack at it, see what comes out. Specifically, I'll try two things

  • Have a version of partial derivatives that we can use with a physics-friendly notation, like \partial_1 f(x_1,x_2,\ldots, x_n)
  • Have some version of differentials that we can also use with a physics-friendly notation. Something like df = \sum_k \partial_k f dx_k

I'll check out what's out there in PhysLib

I already have some notation in my project, it is explained here https://lecopivo.github.io/scientific-computing-lean/Differentiation/Symbolic-Differentiation/#Scientific-Computing-in-Lean--Differentiation--Symbolic-Differentiation--Notation
Physlib also has this notation, which is similar to Tomas'.

Ah, this is almost identical to what I was thinking. The "Space and Time" placing of this feels odd to me, though. I mean, I am building this for thermodynamics and it feels odd to have to import stuff from space and time. My GR brain thinks of Minkowski when I hear Spacetime and I would not have thought of looking into the SpaceAndTime folder without you telling me
I had once wanted to call this WorldVolume but I was voted down on this :joy:. Maybe TimeAndSpace is better?
